newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's tourism business off the boil.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's tourism business off the boil.

text.p: More foreigners flocked to Vietnam than ever before in 1996, but growth in the number of visitors fell by almost half after several years of rapid rises, state-controlled media reports said on Monday.
The National Administration of Tourism declined to confirm the reports, which put the number of foreigners visiting Vietnam this year at a record 1.6 million, up 18 percent from last year.
However, that total was 100,000 short of a government target and compared with growth of 33 percent in 1995.
The government-run Dau Tu magazine said the slowdown could be partly explained by investors' reticence ahead of a mid-year Communist Party congress and a new law on foreign investment.
Hoteliers say they were also hit hard by sudden restrictions on visas in the run-up to the congress.
Although that clampdown has been eased, newspapers said on Monday that the government had now decided to bar foreign travel agencies from organising visas and tours in Vietnam.

"These overseas tourist companies have conducted tours for foreign travellers under the name of local travel agencies," the Saigon Times Daily said, adding that they had cut package prices "to the bone" and could put local agencies out of business.
Dau Tu said natural calamities such as heavy flooding, which this year cost more than 1,200 lives, and the growing hassle of pickpockets and beggars had also deterred many tourists.

"In fact, visitors are suffering from beggars and pickpockets at tourist destinations, and that is a big obstacle for tourist activities," it quoted the tourist administration's General Director, Vo Thi Thang, as saying.

Hue, Vietnam's old imperial capital and one of its most popular tourist destinations, saw a 30-percent drop in visitors this year and the occupancy rate at hotels in Ho Chi Minh City, old Saigon, dropped to 45 percent from 54 percent in 1995.

Vietnam is still a challenging destination for Western tourists because of poor infrastructure, facilities and information, and low-budget backpackers complain that costs are often higher than in other Asian countries.
